title: Curricular Practical Training (CPT) Protocol Effective May 6, 2021
label: Not covered
text: Curricular Practical Training (CPT) Protocol Effective May 6, 2021 | International Student and Scholar Services | University of Colorado Boulder Skip to main content Search Enter the terms you wish to search for. This site All of Colorado.edu Other ways to search: Events Calendar Campus Map Advising Services MyISSS Portal Departmental Services Immigration Alerts & FAQs Curricular Practical Training (CPT) Protocol Effective May 6, 2021 Published:2/1/2021 2/1/2021 Curricular Practical Training (CPT) is a temporary training authorization for an “alternative work/study, internship, cooperative education, or any other type of required internship or practicum which is offered by sponsoring employers through cooperative agreements with the school.” ISSS is updating our Curricular Practical Training (CPT) protocol to ensure that CU Boulder maintains compliance with the Department of Homeland Security F-1 visa regulations and is more closely aligned with the CPT policies of our peer institutions. CPT must be an integral part of your major curriculum, supported by either a credit bearing internship class or required for your major for any CPT authorized for May 6, 2021 or later. You must meet one of the following requirements for CPT, which your major department must sign off on: Be enrolled in an internship course for credit that counts towards your degree. (Enrollment in the course must be concurrent with the training. For example, if the internship is in the summer, you must be enrolled in the internship course during the summer) or Your degree must require an internship and that requirement is clearly documented in the University Catalog . If you do not meet the requirements for the CPT protocol effective May 6, 2021, then you have the option to apply for pre-completion OPT for off-campus work authorization. Please review ISSS’s Pre-completion OPT webpage and ISSS Pre-Completion OPT Guide for information on pre-completion OPT. ISSS understands the impact this change in CPT protocol may have on our international students in F-1 status who would like to take advantage of off-campus training opportunities. However, this change is necessary in order to ensure both CU Boulder and our international students in F-1 status are in compliance with federal rules. ISSS encourages you to attend a CPT Workshop via zoom to learn more about the CPT Protocol Effective May 6th. All sessions take place online via Zoom . February 23, 2021 at 3:30 p.m. March 18, 2021 at 3:30 p.m. April 6, 2021 at 5 p.m. April 29, 2021 at 11 a.m. Further information regarding CPT, including frequently asked questions and answers, is available on the ISSS Curricular Practical Training (CPT) Protocol Effective May 6, 2021 webpage .

text: Groups Tied to Harvard Sue DHS Over New Limits on International Student Internships | The Harvard Crimson The Harvard Crimson Advertisement Advertisement News Groups Tied to Harvard Sue DHS Over New Limits on International Student Internships A coalition of higher education groups with ties to Harvard sued the Department of Homeland Security Monday over new restrictions on Curricular Practical Training for international students. | By E. Matteo Diaz By Sebastian B. Connolly and Summer E. Rose , Crimson Staff Writers A coalition of higher education groups sued the Department of Homeland Security Monday, alleging that two August directives restricting which internships international students can take part in on student visas had caused “irreparable harm” to students and institutions. In a 44-page filing in federal court in Massachusetts, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the DHS had engaged in “procedurally invalid” rulemaking reinterpreting the rules governing Curricular Practical Training — a program allowing international students to participate in internships and experiential learning opportunities — to allow it only for internships that every student in a degree program must complete to graduate. The Student and Exchange Visitor Program, which certifies schools to enroll international students, detailed the interpretation of the rule in two broadcast messages on Aug. 12 and 24. In the messages, SEVP officials framed the update as a reminder of existing policy — and warned that universities could lose their SEVP certification, which would bar them from hosting students on visas. The Aug. 12 message also warned that improper authorizations could expose individual school officials, not just their institutions, to “administrative or legal consequences.” In Monday’s suit, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the broadcasts are “impermissibly retroactive,” exposing those officials to “criminal prosecution” for past conduct that complied with the government’s position at the time. But in Monday’s filing, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the messages broke with more than 35 years of precedent in how the rule had been interpreted — and were an attempt to introduce new legislative rules without abiding by federal procedure governing administrative action. Harvard has ties to all four plaintiffs in the Monday suit: the Association of American Universities, Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts. The University is a member of AAU, AICUM, and the Presidents’ Alliance, and staff in the Harvard International Office are NAFSA members. Harvard is among several universities to have halted CPT authorizations following the August messages. Five of its schools — Harvard College, Harvard Law School, Harvard Medical School, the Graduate School of Design, and the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences — no longer authorize CPT, and the HIO updated its website to reflect the new guidance. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology, University of Pennsylvania, and Wellesley College are among the schools that have paused authorization of CPT applications since the messages were issued. Get The Crimson in your inbox. Sign up The complaint asks a judge to “restore” the previous interpretation, which allowed students to use CPT for internships taken for academic credit, arguing that the change had already harmed students and schools. “Action is needed now,” the lawyers wrote. “Students have already lost critical internship and research opportunities for the current semester and institutions have had to scramble to determine how ongoing practicums, internships extended from last summer, and applications for future internships might be impacted.” In a separate motion filed Monday night, the plaintiffs asked the court to block DHS from enforcing the new interpretation while the case proceeds. A DHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment The August messages come after a series of federal moves to tighten restrictions on international students. In July, DHS announced a rule that would place a fixed four-year limit on student visas and restrict students’ ability to switch programs. Three of the plaintiffs in Monday’s complaint — the Presidents’ Alliance, NAFSA, and AICUM — are suing to block the rule. On Sept. 14, a day before the rule was set to take effect, a federal judge temporarily blocked it. The government has since appealed the ruling, and the case is ongoing. Advertisement Harvard is engaged in its own lawsuit over the Trump administration’s attempt in May 2025 to revoke its SEVP certification — a case that plaintiffs cited in their separate Monday memorandum seeking an injunction noting that a federal judge had recognized evidence that losing SEVP certification can “irreparably harm” a university. The judge in that case blocked the revocation with a preliminary injunction in June 2025. The government filed a stipulation in August 2025, saying it would decline to enforce the May ruling. —Staff writer Sebastian B. Connolly can be reached at [email protected] or on Signal at sbc.23. title: Higher ed leaders sue Trump administration over limitations on international student internships

text: Higher education leaders file lawsuit against ICE over international student internship restrictions Skip to main content Higher ed leaders sue Trump administration over limitations on international student internships Print this Article View Comments The Moakley Federal Courthouse on Boston Harbor Lane Turner/Globe Staff A coalition of higher education leaders filed a lawsuit Monday in Boston challenging the federal government’s recent interpretation of an internship program for international students, which plaintiffs say will limit student access to work experience and weaken America’s edge in talent recruitment. The lawsuit comes in response to messages US Immigration and Customs Enforcement emailed to university administrators in August that abruptly shifted the requirements for Curricular Practical Training (CPT), a program that allows international students to participate in internships, co-ops, and other temporary work programs related to their studies. The messages declared that students will only be eligible for CPT if the work opportunity is a graduation requirement for all students in a particular degree program, regardless of citizenship. “This action is yet another attempt by the [Trump] administration to dissuade talented international students from continuing their education in America,” Rob McCarron, president of the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, one of the plaintiffs in the case, said in a statement. When contacted by The Boston Globe, an ICE spokesperson said the agency does not comment on pending litigation. According to statistics from ICE , 130,586 foreign students obtained work authorization through CPT in 2024. The top employers of CPT participants in that year included Amazon, Tesla, and Google. Some universities have already limited CPT authorizations ahead of the fall 2026 semester; Harvard University , Massachusetts Institute of Technology , Boston University , Tufts University , and Suffolk University are among the Massachusetts schools that have all temporarily paused most new and pending CPT authorization requests. All five schools are members of AICUM. Several schools in the University of California system, such as the University of California Berkeley , have paused their course-credit work experiences altogether. The Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, another plaintiff in the new case, claimed that some students have already lost work positions they secured months prior as a result of these institutional changes. McCarron, president of the independent colleges group, said the ICE messages have caused “substantial disruptions” on campuses across Massachusetts as schools were forced to abruptly readapt longstanding processes surrounding student work experiences. In the messages sent Aug. 12 and 24, ICE claims that the Student and Exchange Visitor Program has observed a rise in schools issuing CPT authorizations that violate the requirement that work experience to be an “integral part of an established curriculum.” While the text of the regulatory requirements for CPT has not changed, it seems ICE’s interpretation of the word “integral” has shifted. The ICE messages warned that any institution found in violation could be investigated and lose certification to enroll international students. The plaintiffs said the new interpretation of CPT requirements has left long-standing campus practices like co-op programs in limbo without allowing adequate time for schools to respond or take public comment. The lawsuit also alleges that the communications were sent directly to campus university designated school officials — the employees in charge of advising international students and ensuring the university’s compliance with law — and threatened them with institutional penalties and personal liability for allowing previous CPT practices to continue. The lawsuit includes a motion for a preliminary injunction to force the government to stop any changes to CPT immediately, and as long as the case is active. The Presidents’ Alliance and several other plaintiffs in the case previously sued the Department of Homeland Security over limits on how long international students can stay on certain visas; a case that is ongoing. Chloe Craft can be reached at chloe.craft@globe.com .

text: New federal CPT guidelines leave international students across the U.S. without work New federal CPT guidelines leave international students across the U.S. without work 1 month 1 week 2 days ago Friday, August 28 2026 Aug 28, 2026 August 28, 2026 1:04 PM August 28, 2026 in News Source: WBRZ By: WBRZ Staff Share: BATON ROUGE — Universities around the country were issued new guidelines on Monday regarding Curricular Practical Training programs, causing many students enrolled in programs to lose their jobs. CPTs allow students to obtain a part-time job in their area of study and are the only way many international students can legally work while in school. The new guidelines come as the Student and Exchange Visitor Program observed a rise in CPT authorizations that appear to violate regulatory requirements, which permit CPT only where the training is an integral part of an established curriculum. SEVP noted that several institutions throughout the country have described CPT as an optional practical training despite clear regulatory requirements. CPTs that are classified as optional would fail to meet the integral and required aspects for authorization under the new guidelines. It was also discovered that some institutions have not required all students enrolled in the same established curriculum to participate in practical training. Here are the highlights: A consortium of sector stakeholders is suing the US government over recent guidance that has curtailed Curricular Practical Training placements for international students The plaintiffs claim that the administration sidestepped a proper rulemaking process to threaten or potentially impose sanctions on US institutions, and they are seeking to have the longstanding CPT framework restored The Department of Homeland Security has also issued a notice of proposed rulemaking, with the proposed rule to be officially published on 8 October The rule sets out a US$70,000 fee for Optional Practical Training, with an additional US$30,000 levy for OPT extensions Given the importance of OPT to international students in the US, it seems likely that it too will be robustly challenged In two broadcast memos issued in August 2026, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement department (ICE) clearly signalled that it is now applying greater scrutiny to Curricular Practical Training (CPT) placements . CPT allows a student to complete an internship or practicum offered by a sponsoring employer through a co-operative agreement with the student’s school, and ICE says that the Student and Visa Exchange Programme (SEVP) is showing an uptick in “CPT authorisations that do not meet regulatory requirements, specifically those not constituting an integral part of an established curriculum.” The agency warned that if institutions are suspected of using CPT inappropriately – namely to create work opportunities rather than for the sake of academics – then they could be subject to additional action, including the "potential withdrawal of the school’s SEVP certification.” The fallout from those memos was immediate with many institutions around the country promptly pausing their authorisation of elective CPT programmes. Back to court The matter has now entered the legal arena with notice this week of a lawsuit brought by several sector stakeholders. On 5 October, the Association of American Universities (AAU), Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA, and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts filed a legal action against ICE, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of Justice. The lawsuit sets out: "On the eve of a new academic year and semester, [DHS] abruptly changed a position that the federal government had held for more than thirty-five years and sharply restricted international students’ access to internships and other hands-on learning opportunities – all while simultaneously threatening college and university officials with criminal prosecution for approving enrolments consistent with the government’s prior longstanding policy. This sudden change was issued with no substantive explanation, opportunity for comment, or even acknowledgement of the change, but with maximal impact on affected students and institutions." The filing goes on to argue that "DHS’s actions should be promptly stayed and enjoined given their many legal flaws and the ongoing harms they inflict on colleges and universities, their officials, and their students." “We are going to court to protect our students and institutions,” said Presidents’ Alliance President and CEO Miriam Feldblum. “ICE’s broadcast messages announced a change to longstanding CPT requirements and threatened serious consequences for campus staff and institutions. Colleges and universities across the country have paused or halted CPT authorizations, and students have already lost internships and other placements. We are asking the court to act swiftly to stop the government’s actions and restore the longstanding CPT framework that campuses and international students have relied on for decades to plan academic programs and practical training.” Join 37,000 subscribers and stay up to date on International Recruitment Subscribe For Free “Changing how CPT is administered through broadcast messages, without formal rulemaking, is an aberration that must be challenged,” added NAFSA Executive Director and CEO Fanta Aw. “These abrupt changes have placed Designated School Officials – the professionals responsible for advising international students and ensuring institutional compliance – in an untenable position, forcing them to navigate significant new restrictions and uncertainty without the clarity and due process that formal rulemaking provides. Hands-on, experiential learning is a hallmark of a US education, and restricting access to it in this way is already disrupting opportunities for international students. The consequences extend well beyond individual students and campuses. Driving away international student talent will have long-term consequences for US research, innovation, workforce development, and global competitiveness.” The plaintiffs say they are seeking to restore the longstanding CPT framework, and, in so doing to protect students and institutions from retroactive penalties and ensure that meaningful training opportunities remain available to visiting students. title: What suspended Curricular Practical Training means for international students
label: Not covered
text: What suspended Curricular Practical Training means for international students – The Wellesley News Skip to Content What suspended Curricular Practical Training means for international students Alicia Zhang , Contributing Writer | October 8, 2026 Photo Courtesy of The New York Times A rally for international students at Harvard University On Sept. 28 of this year, a letter from President Paula Johnson to the international students changed the educational trajectory of students at Wellesley College. The letter announced an indefinite pause on Curricular Practical Training (CPT), a temporary work authorization that lets international students on F-1 visas have the opportunity to seek off-campus practical work experience. With CPT no longer being an option, international students will need to rely heavily on the two experiential learning requirement (ELR) credits that allow them to pursue internships and research experiences. In a political environment that becomes increasingly hostile to international students, Wellesley’s ELR requirement carries sobering implications. Effective for students arriving at Wellesley in fall 2024 and beyond, the ELR asks students to complete two units before their senior year, fulfilled by either one summer-long or two semester-long experiences. By including a variety of choices — from internships and on-campus jobs to community service and civic engagement — the ELR encourages students to develop a well-rounded portfolio for future degrees and careers. However, after CPT was paused, if an international student has already fulfilled the two ELR units, any research or internship opportunities are not authorized. This is an issue especially for upperclassmen who have already completed certain fellowships and CareerEd programs that have automatically counted toward their ELR units. What was initially designed to encourage students to engage in various career-preparatory opportunities has now become a tight thing to manage. This abrupt policy change leaves current international students at a disadvantage. Additionally, future students may choose only two research or internship experiences to count toward their two required ELR units, rather than considering other valuable opportunities. The suspension of CPT was driven by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) , a direct program division within the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). SEVP’s increased scrutiny of CPT approvals was justified by the claim that it “has observed a rise in CPT authorizations that do not meet regulatory requirements, specifically those not constituting an integral part of an established curriculum.” From SEVP’s perspective, only those experiences directly required for obtaining a degree count as “ an integral part of an established curriculum ,” which gives the ludicrous implication that any additional learning is unnecessary and — more problematically — prohibited by the U.S. government. The politically charged statements given by SEVP confirm the blatant assault on the international student community: “DSOs [Designated School Officials] are reminded that F nonimmigrant students are, by their own attestation under penalty of perjury, here in the United States ‘solely for the purpose of pursuing a full program of study.’” Universities are also threatened with “additional scrutiny and action from SEVP and Homeland Security Investigations” if “SEVP suspects that school officials are abusing CPT to create work opportunities rather than academic studies.” The long promised opportunity in American higher education is vilified as an abuse of CPT. The distinct separation of “academic studies” from “work opportunities” also reflects the political agenda of limiting opportunities for foreigners to stay in the country. The discontinuation of CPT is not the first attack on international students; it is the culmination of cutthroat policies that have pushed international students into dreadful struggles. Earlier this July, Trump issued a Final Rule to eliminate the long-standing “duration of status” admission for J-1 Exchange Visitors and F-1 students. Although this rule has been blocked by a federal judge, if it were to take effect, it would create significant hassles for international students who need more than four years to complete their enrolled program or degree. Moreover, it demonstrates Trump’s antagonism toward international students and immigrants. This goes hand in hand with the CPT suspens ion and depriving international students of a chance to extend learning beyond their degree. International students make up roughly 14% of Wellesley’s student body; nationwide, 1.2 million international students are affected by current hostile policies. This part of the Wellesley community includes some of the most vulnerable students, yet these students receive less support than they deserve. The College, for example, could make ELR more flexible to help international students seize the academic and career opportunities they urgently need. Giving students the autonomy to choose which experiences count towards the two required units could be one pragmatic solution. Overall, there should be stronger support systems in place to help international students fight back against the consequences of volatile policy shifts.
